title: Thymosin β4 and BPC-157 as Candidate Regenerative Peptide Therapies for Spinal Cord Injury: Mechanisms, Preclinical Evidence, and First Clinical Signals
content: Spinal cord injury (SCI) remains without an approved pharmacological therapy capable of restoring lost neurological function, and recovery in motor-complete, sensory-incomplete (AIS B) patients is constrained by a limited spontaneous-conversion profile. Two regenerative peptides have assembled convergent preclinical rationales in SCI. Thymosin β4 (Tβ4), the principal G-actin-sequestering peptide of eukaryotic cells, promotes oligodendrogenesis, axonal remodeling, angiogenesis, and anti-inflammatory signalling, and has improved functional recovery in rodent SCI. The stable gastric pentadecapeptide BPC-157 acts chiefly through VEGFR2 upregulation and the Akt–eNOS nitric-oxide axis, and has produced consistent functional recovery in rat SCI models. This review synthesises the molecular pharmacology of both agents, the preclinical SCI literature, the limited human exposure data, and the safety and regulatory context, including the important distinction between full-length Tβ4 and the synthetic fragment TB-500. It then examines the first clinical signal: a 6-month open-label controlled pilot in subacute AIS-B thoracic SCI in which weekly subcutaneous Tβ4 plus BPC-157, added to intensive rehabilitation, was associated with larger motor, sensory, trunk, and autonomic gains than rehabilitation alone, with only mild adverse effects. The evidence base remains preclinical-first and hypothesis-generating; the design requirements for a confirmatory trial are outlined. Neither peptide is approved for SCI, and both are subject to significant regulatory restrictions.
